question: What does zāgha mean here?

positions.position: To deviate or turn aside from the intended course.
positions.reasons: Majāz and Ibn Qutayba give the basic sense; Mwardī reports deviation; Bursevī specifies deviation from uprightness; Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies the intended course; Sāmarrāʾī says either side. Jishumī applies it to turning from sought truth; Ṭabāṭabāʾī gives deviation from uprightness as the root sense.

positions.position: For the sight to go away.
positions.reasons: Māwardī attributes this explanation to Ibn ʿAbbās.

positions.position: Deficiency or falling short.
positions.reasons: Māwardī attributes this explanation to Ibn Baḥr, who then denies deficient comprehension in the Prophet's vision.

positions.position: In the case of sight, to perceive inaccurately.
positions.reasons: Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes the visual application from the general sense of deviation; Rāzī also denies seeing things contrary to reality.

turns_on: Whether zaygh names a change of direction, loss or deficiency of vision, or error in perception.

question: What does ṭaghā mean here?

positions.position: To increase or cross a limit.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba says increase or exceed; Ibn Baḥr says increase; Ibn ʿĀshūr and Sāmarrāʾī specify crossing the limit or looking beyond what is allowed; Ṭabāṭabāʾī gives exceeding a limit as the basic sense.

positions.position: To rise above or go beyond the truth.
positions.reasons: Māwardī gives the first wording and transmits the second from Ibn ʿAbbās.

positions.position: To seek unjust elevation over another.
positions.reasons: Jishumī compares ṭāghī with bāghī.

positions.position: For sight, to perceive something unreal.
positions.reasons: Ṭabāṭabāʾī applies the sense of excess to vision; Rāzī similarly denies imagining a nonexistent thing as real.

turns_on: Whether the excess is of a limit, of truth, of status over another, or of visual perception.

question: Whose sight is al-baṣar?

positions.position: Muhammad's sight.
positions.reasons: Rāzī reads the article as identifying his sight; Ṭabāṭabāʾī states the referent explicitly. The Ibn ʿAbbās reports and the common explanations likewise attach the gaze to the Prophet; Ibn ʿĀshūr says he saw Gabriel.

positions.position: Sight generically: no eye veered under the awe.
positions.reasons: Rāzī reports the alternative and observes that a definite noun under negation can have generic scope, citing 6:103.

turns_on: Whether the definite article singles out the Prophet's eye or gives the negated noun generic scope.

question: What did the gaze not turn away from?

positions.position: It did not wander right or left from what was before it.
positions.reasons: Farrāʾ, Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAbbās as reported by Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr and Durr describe lateral movement; Wāḥidī calls it a sideways glance. ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās adds that God enabled him to look without fear or panic; Elmalılı and Kur'an Yolu stress the astonishing scene.

positions.position: It did not turn from the particular object, signs, or wonders shown to him.
positions.reasons: Zajjāj identifies Gabriel filling the horizon. Qushayrī, Wāḥidī, Ṭabrisī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān transmitting Zamakhsharī, Bursevī, Ālūsī and Study Quran refer to the permitted or commanded signs; Ibn ʿĀshūr speaks of Gabriel. Rāzī says moths or locusts at the Sidra did not divert him; on the lights reading, he did not turn from those lights.

positions.position: It did not turn from God toward anything else, even himself.
positions.reasons: Tustarī says absorption in the Lord and His manifest attributes excluded self-witnessing; Qāshānī excludes another object and selfhood. Rāzī's moths reading excludes anything besides God; al-Kāshifī speaks of everlasting divine beauty, al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya of the divine names and attributes instead of worldly or otherworldly attractions, and al-Baqlī of refusing even a noble distraction in the second vision.

positions.position: It did not turn from the truth sought.
positions.reasons: Jishumī defines zaygh as turning aside from sought truth; Ṭūsī, reported by Study Quran, applies the line to the Prophet's pursuit of truth.

positions.position: It did not perceive the seen thing falsely.
positions.reasons: Rāzī denies perception contrary to reality; Ṭabāṭabāʾī denies inaccurate sight; Elmalılı says it did not see falsely.

turns_on: Whether the point is lateral motion, attention to the shown object, exclusive attention to God or truth, or fidelity of perception.

question: What did the gaze not exceed?

positions.position: It did not look past the object it actually saw.
positions.reasons: Farrāʾ, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī speak of stopping at the seen object; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say this confirms the event and removes doubt. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the sight did not exceed what was described.

positions.position: It did not look beyond what God commanded or permitted him to see.
positions.reasons: Naḥḥās says it did not pass what he could discern; Ibn ʿAbbās via Wāḥidī and Durr says what was commanded. Others specify permitted signs or bounds; Ibn Kathīr extends the restraint to asking for nothing more than was given. Ṭūsī says it held whether the vision concerned Gabriel or God; Sāmarrāʾī says the scene's pull did not move it.

positions.position: It did not exceed the truth by making the vision larger or unreal.
positions.reasons: Māwardī gives going beyond truth and Ibn Baḥr excludes excess imagined in perception; Rāzī denies imagining the nonexistent. Elmalılı and Ṭabāṭabāʾī connect the limit with sound perception.

positions.position: It did not turn inward to selfhood.
positions.reasons: Qāshānī makes the excess an inward turning toward oneself that would veil the vision.

turns_on: Whether the boundary is the seen object, a commanded allowance, truthful perception, or selfless attention.

question: What does the verse affirm about the accuracy of the vision?

positions.position: The Prophet saw truly and with certainty, without deficiency, excess, illusion, or exaggeration.
positions.reasons: Ibn Baḥr denies deficient comprehension and imagined excess; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say the fixed gaze confirms the event and dispels doubt; Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī stress certainty. Rāzī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī deny false perception, Elmalılı precise observation, and Ibn ʿĀshūr says the verse restates 53:13–18 and denies exaggeration. Iṣlāḥī says revelatory experience of Gabriel is no illusion.

positions.position: The verse marks the Prophet's ability to observe the signs without becoming bewildered.
positions.reasons: ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās says God strengthened him against fear; Rāzī contrasts possible unconsciousness before divine lights; Ibn Kathīr cites a poet saying he saw the Garden of Abode and what was above it, and another sight would have bewildered him.

turns_on: Whether the stress falls on objective truth of what was seen or on his capacity to see it steadily.

question: What quality of the Prophet does the verse praise?

positions.position: Proper etiquette and obedient restraint before the divine presence.
positions.reasons: Qushayrī, Wāḥidī, Wāḥidī's Wajīz, Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Qurṭubī, Bursevī via Kāshifī, Elmalılı, Kur'an Yolu and Sāmarrāʾī call this decorum; Ibn Kathīr says he did only what was commanded and sought no more; Biqāʿī calls it just, chaste moderation amid wonders.

positions.position: Unshaken strength and composure before overwhelming sights.
positions.reasons: Rāzī compares steady sight before divine lights to composure before a king and says he did not lose consciousness; Elmalılı and Kur'an Yolu contrast Moses' collapse. Kur'an Yolu reads the second verb as strength of gaze.

positions.position: Exact, certain perception.
positions.reasons: Ibn Baḥr denies perceptual shortfall and addition; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says accurate sight confirms the event; Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī emphasize certainty; Rāzī calls the certainty unsurpassed.

positions.position: Complete devotion, free from self and lesser attractions.
positions.reasons: Tustarī says absorption in the Lord steadied the Prophet; Qāshānī rejects attention to others or self; Kāshifī praises high aspiration; al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya says bodily and spiritual sight ignored worldly and afterlife rewards; al-Baqlī calls this the beloved's steadfast wish to behold his Lord.

turns_on: The notes draw distinct, compatible inferences from a steady gaze: manners, strength, accuracy, and inward devotion.

question: What was the object of the vision in this passage?

positions.position: Gabriel in his true form or the divine signs shown through him.
positions.reasons: Zajjāj identifies Gabriel filling the horizon; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the Prophet saw Gabriel and that 53:13–18 restates the sight. Study Quran reports a common interpretation of two visions of Gabriel in true form, unlike his usual human appearance; Ṭabāṭabāʾī observes that the passage names signs and revelation, not God.

positions.position: God was seen.
positions.reasons: Bursevī infers a waking sight of God with physical eyes; al-Baqlī treats this as the second vision of the beloved looking to his Lord. Study Quran reports that many locate a vision of God during the Night Journey and Ascension, by heart alone or by eye and heart.

positions.position: The verse leaves the seen object open between Gabriel and God.
positions.reasons: Ṭūsī says the prohibition on seeking more holds with either object. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says even a hypothetical vision of God would be heart-sight, while the passage itself names God's great signs; the poet cited by Ibn Kathīr specifies the Garden of Abode and what lay above it as sights.

turns_on: Whether the nearby descriptions identify Gabriel, the great signs, or a vision of God.

question: Was this sight physical eye-sight or heart-vision?

positions.position: The Prophet saw God with physical eyes while awake.
positions.reasons: Bursevī prefers this: naming the eye as steady suggests waking vision; a heart-vision would have named the heart. Study Quran reports that some readers combine eye and heart sight.

positions.position: It was heart-vision.
positions.reasons: Ṭabāṭabāʾī links this seeing to 53:11 and 53:13 and says that even if God were the object, seeing God would be heart-sight rather than bodily sensory vision; Study Quran reports readers of a heart-only vision. Bursevī acknowledges the inner-sight construal as possible in isolation but rejects it for lack of contextual evidence.

positions.position: Baṣar could mean inner sight, though the context does not support it here.
positions.reasons: Bursevī records the lexical possibility only to reject it because the passage gives no contextual evidence.

turns_on: Whether baṣar and the surrounding wording signal bodily waking sight or the inner vision linked to 53:11–13.

question: What does the definite article in al-baṣar imply?

positions.position: It identifies Muhammad's particular sight.
positions.reasons: Rāzī ties the individual eye to the Sidra scene: whether insects or lights covered it, his sight stayed on its purpose.

positions.position: It gives generic scope: no sight veered under the awe.
positions.reasons: Rāzī reports this alternative and replies that a definite noun under negation can be generic, citing 6:103.

turns_on: Whether the definite noun points to the Prophet specifically or has universal force under negation.

question: How can the second clause be construed syntactically?

positions.position: It may stand as an independent sentence.
positions.reasons: Rāzī gives this as one construction.

positions.position: Its subject may be omitted and supplied from the first clause.
positions.reasons: Rāzī gives this as the alternative construction.

turns_on: Whether the second clause has independent force or depends on an understood subject.

question: Why mention sight and choose these two verbs?

positions.position: Sight signals an immense encounter met by steady composure.
positions.reasons: Rāzī contrasts sight with heart and likens the Prophet to one composed before a king; Bursevī uses the mention of eye to infer waking sight.

positions.position: The verbs make looking aside or beyond blameworthy there.
positions.reasons: Rāzī says the choice of zaygh and ṭughyān carries censure and marks unsurpassed certainty; Kur'an Yolu assigns courtesy to the first verb and strength of gaze to the second.

turns_on: Whether the wording chiefly emphasizes the faculty that endured the encounter or the moral force of the two verbs.

question: How is the scene compared with Moses' experience?

positions.position: Muhammad and the Sidra remained steady where Moses collapsed and the mountain was shattered.
positions.reasons: Rāzī compares the divine lights with Moses' loss of consciousness; Elmalılı and Kur'an Yolu cite Moses at 7:143 and contrast the standing Sidra and composed Prophet. Kashf al-Asrār adds that Moses asked to see God, heard 'You will not see Me', and repented, whereas Muhammad's divinely guarded gaze is praised, invoking 7:143 and 20:131.

question: When is this vision placed in the Prophet's life?

positions.position: It belongs to the Night Journey and Ascension toward the end of the Meccan period.
positions.reasons: Wāḥidī's Wajīz sets the conduct on the Night Journey; Kur'an Yolu says the sūra is early Meccan but 53:13–18 are generally tied to the later Miʿrāj. Study Quran says they may be later than the sūra's early setting, and many date the Ascension most likely to 619.

positions.position: The Ascension occurred in 614, seven years before the hijrah.
positions.reasons: Study Quran reports a minority dating.

turns_on: The reported dates of the Ascension differ, although both place it in Meccan time.

question: What does the Gabriel report say happened at the ascent?

positions.position: Muhammad saw Gabriel in his true form a second time; Gabriel then prostrated.
positions.reasons: A report tentatively attributed to Ibn Masʿūd says the first true-form sight followed Muhammad's request and filled the horizon; the second was at the ascent, when Gabriel resumed his form and prostrated. It calls Gabriel's creation the great signs. Aḥmad transmits it, and Ibn Kathīr calls it strange.

positions.position: The passage describes two visions of Gabriel in his true form.
positions.reasons: Study Quran says many commentators distinguish these visions from Gabriel's usual human appearance.

turns_on: Whether to state the general two-vision identification or the detailed, unusually graded Ibn Masʿūd report.

question: How does this passage support the sūra's account of revelation?

positions.position: It validates revelation through the trustworthy angel against claims of invention, soothsaying, and illusion.
positions.reasons: Iṣlāḥī says 53:1–18 establish the Qur'an as revelation from God's dependable angel and deny soothsaying and fortune-telling; he also denies illusory revelatory experiences. Study Quran relates the opening to the disbelievers' allegation in 52:33 that the Prophet invented revelation and notes the opening's rhetorical power and disputed interpretation.

positions.position: The scene directs faith beyond the senses and limits speculative reason.
positions.reasons: Kur'an Yolu draws this lesson from the mysterious, vivid scene.

positions.position: It undercuts pagan attempts to assign divinity to intermediaries.
positions.reasons: Kur'an Yolu says the passage condemns making divinity concrete through material or spiritual beings and attributing godhood besides God.

turns_on: Whether the passage's main polemical force is authentication of revelation, restraint of speculation, or denial of intermediary gods.

question: What additional scriptural parallel is drawn with Joseph?

positions.position: Muhammad's pardon of his Meccan kin echoes Joseph's pardon of his brothers.
positions.reasons: Biqāʿī cites Joseph's words in 12:92 as the model for the pardon at the conquest.

question: What does the ancillary report say about the Prophet's speech?

positions.position: A phrase or two of his speech can gather many matters from earlier books.
positions.reasons: Ibn Abī Shihāb, reported in al-Itqān, explains the Prophet's description of his speech as comprehensive.
